articles.title: Elon Musk wants to combine Tesla and SpaceX. But would investors benefit?
articles.summary: By Joe Brock Oct 21 (Reuters) - Elon Musk believes a merger between Tesla and SpaceX is a good idea, he said on Tuesday, publicly backing an idea that would create one of the most valuable companies in the world, worth about $3.5 trillion. While electric-vehicle maker Tesla and rocket company SpaceX ‌were once seen as largely separate businesses, the lines between them have blurred as Musk expands into artificial intelligence, robotics, advanced manufacturing, satellite communications, and ‌computing infrastructure, including data centers on Earth and potentially in orbit. Here's what a potential merger could mean: WHY WOULD MUSK DO THIS? A merger would create a single company at the center of Musk's long-term vision: an ​integrated technology and manufacturing empire spanning AI, energy, robotics, communications, and transportation on Earth and beyond. "I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation (of orbital data centers), connectivity," Musk said on Tuesday. Bringing the companies together could also simplify decision-making. Many of Musk's projects already cut across multiple companies, requiring approvals from separate boards and shareholders. ‌A combined company would give management more freedom to deploy ⁠capital, engineering talent and infrastructure where it sees the greatest opportunity. Musk has long argued that he needs greater influence over Tesla to pursue its AI and robotics strategy. He owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and holds voting control at SpaceX. A merger could consolidate ⁠his influence. WHAT DOES IT MEAN FOR INVESTORS? Tesla shareholders would gain access to SpaceX's rapidly growing Starlink broadband operation, launch services business and future space ventures. SpaceX investors would gain ownership of Tesla's vehicle, energy storage, autonomous driving and robotics businesses. A merged company could also become one of the world's most valuable corporations, with a market value of about $3.5 trillion, combining leadership positions in ​automobiles, ​robotics, satellite communications, launch services, energy storage and AI infrastructure. Supporters would likely argue that the combined ​company could allocate capital more efficiently across businesses that are increasingly ‌interdependent. Critics, however, argue that investors would be assuming exposure to a much broader range of technical, regulatory and execution risks, some of which have little connection to one another. WHERE COULD SPACEX AND TESLA WORK TOGETHER? Starlink satellites could provide communications links for Tesla's robotaxis, autonomous systems and future generations of Optimus humanoid robots. Tesla's battery and energy-storage products could help support SpaceX's growing power needs, including future data-center projects. Musk has already announced one major Tesla-SpaceX collaboration, Terafab, a semiconductor and AI-computing project aimed at producing the advanced chips needed for Tesla's autonomous vehicles and Optimus robots, as well as SpaceX's AI and data-center ambitions. Musk hopes it can start volume production by late 2028. Tesla's expertise in large-scale ‌factory automation could complement SpaceX's efforts to industrialize Starship production, while SpaceX technologies have already appeared in ​Tesla products, most notably the planned use of rocket-derived components in the next-generation Roadster. A merged company could ​also coordinate efforts to secure strategic supply chains, leveraging Tesla's scale in batteries, ​semiconductors and manufacturing equipment alongside SpaceX's demand for specialized metals, electronics, propulsion components and satellite hardware. WHAT ARE THE DOWNSIDE RISKS? The biggest challenges ‌may be geopolitics and regulation. SpaceX is a major contractor for the US ​military, intelligence agencies and NASA. Tesla, meanwhile, ​remains deeply tied to China through its Shanghai factory, which plays a major role in vehicle production and sales. That combination could invite heightened scrutiny from US regulators and national-security officials as well as from Beijing. The merger would also face shareholder and governance hurdles. Investors would need to be persuaded that combining ​two already complex businesses creates more value than keeping them ‌separate. Questions about conflicts of interest, voting control and capital allocation would inevitably follow. Then there is execution risk. Starship, robotaxis, humanoid robots, AI data centers, ​mobile communications and orbital infrastructure are all expensive, technically challenging bets. Combining Tesla and SpaceX would not reduce those risks. It would simply place ​them under one roof. (Reporting by Joe Brock; Editing by Peter Henderson and Sonali Paul) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://finance.yahoo.com/news/explainer-why-musk-merge-spacex-020904506.html

articles.title: Russia releases imprisoned American as U.S. envoy meets with Putin
articles.summary: Russia on Wednesday released a retired American teacher who had been imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said Wednesday at a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg. The release of Stephen Hubbard had been foreshadowed a day earlier in Washington, when President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that he had talked with Putin “at length” about the issue and had asked him to free the Michigan man. Hubbard is the second American detainee in just over two months to be freed by Russia, and his exit from custody occurred not only during a visit by Witkoff but also at a time when Trump has taken a series of actions meant to benefit Russia as Washington's alliance with Ukraine shows signs of fraying. Hubbard was sentenced after a closed trial in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison. Prosecutors said he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military after Russia sent troops into Ukraine in February 2022, and that he fought alongside them until being captured two months later. The U.S. government under the Biden administration designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained. Witkoff , a key Trump administration envoy who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end a war that will hit the five-year mark in February , thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard, telling him, “Because of you, he's going home to his family.” The Russian leader responded that Hubbard was at the St. Petersburg airport, Pulkovo, after the release. The release occurred at a dynamic moment in relations between the United States, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv alliance being stretched by tensions over drone support as the Trump administration advances policies that aid Putin. Trump decided Friday, for instance, to waive sanctions on Russia in a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine. Named after late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham , the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fueling Russia’s war. That reversal followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections next month. Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday. He was expected to exchange ideas from that meeting, as well as proposals from European and American colleagues, in his talks with Russian leaders in St. Petersburg on Wednesday. Hubbard is the second American freed by Russia in about the last two months, following the release in August of Marine veteran Robert Gilman , who had been gravely ill and was imprisoned on disputed charges of assaulting a police officer. Some two dozen Americans remain imprisoned in Russia for various reasons, according to the Foley Foundation, a hostage advocacy organization. Hubbard had been imprisoned since 2022 on charges that Hostage Aid Worldwide, a hostage advocacy group, has called bogus. The organization in August posted an open letter to Trump that it said was written by Patricia Hubbard Fox, Hubbard’s sister, in which she offered praise for Trump but also said brother had been subjected to “constant beatings, torture and starvation” while in custody. “Even so, everything that you’re doing isn’t going to matter to my kidnapped, American Veteran brother, Stephen James Hubbard (soon to be 74) if Putin won’t cave and let him come home and he dies up there in a Nazi prison (crying),” the letter said. _____ Tucker reported from Washington. articles.title: At least 9 more lawmakers say they were targets of suspicious mail
articles.summary: U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., said Tuesday that one of her district offices was mailed a suspicious envelope. Pool Photo by Adam Gray/UPI Oct. 21 (UPI) -- At least nine U.S. lawmakers announced Tuesday that suspicious envelopes had been mailed to their offices, the latest in a wave of similar mailings targeting federal legislators from both parties in the past week. More than three dozen senators and House members have reported receiving suspicious envelopes, some containing white powder or unknown substances, or having them intercepted by postal investigators. The mailings were first reported Oct. 13, when suspicious letters were received by the offices of elected officials in Louisiana and Oklahoma. On Tuesday, lawmakers who announced letters had been sent to their offices included Reps. Nanette Barragán, D-Calif.; Shontel Brown, D-Ohio; Jim Costa, D-Calif.; Robert Garcia, D-Calif.; Pablo José Hernández, D-P.R.; Donald Norcross, D-N.J.; and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.; and Sens. Jim Banks, R-Ind.; and Deb Fischer, R-Neb. "This string of suspicious mailings started two weeks before a consequential midterm election and is seemingly intended to intimidate public servants and sow further division," Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement Tuesday, announcing that a suspicious letter had been delivered to her district office in Hunts Point. "Political violence has no place in our country. It is always unacceptable and we must all refuse to normalize an unsafe and volatile political environment where everyday people are put at risk." Pictures of the letters posted online by some lawmakers in the past week show that the intended recipients' names and addresses are handwritten, while the return addresses are printed and in some cases identical: a New York City address formerly used by the Democratic Socialists of America, a political organization that has denied involvement with the letters. There have been no reported injuries and federal and local authorities are investigating. No arrests have been announced. On Monday, House Sergeant at Arms William McFarland sent lawmakers a memo obtained by Roll Call stating, "none of the letters received by congressional offices have been determined to contain hazardous substances," but that more offices could receive similar letters "in the coming days." That same day, more than a dozen lawmakers said suspicious letters had been sent to their offices. "A single threat against one elected official is chilling enough. But it's more common than ever that elected officials and their staff -- no matter their title nor party -- are being targeted for no other reason than choosing public service," Norcross said in a statement Tuesday, announced that a suspicious envelope addressed to his Cherry Hill district office had been intercepted by postal service investigators a day prior. "That's unsustainable for any version of a healthy, functional government." articles.title: Childcare costs are weighing on voters, and they could help decide control of Congress
articles.summary: Like so many Americans, Jenny Escolastico has watched wearily as the cost of living has risen, straining her household budget. But as a mother of two children under 5, she faces added pressure that could shape how she votes in November : childcare costs. Escolastico’s household outside Allentown, Pennsylvania, is relying solely on her husband’s income. She’s staying home with her children, at least in part because she simply can’t afford to work . "What I would be spending on childcare would be more than what I would be making if I were working full time,” said Escolastico, an Air Force veteran who later worked in human resources. “Childcare is another rent, another car note.” Even though her son now attends state-funded prekindergarten , returning to work would still mean finding him after-school care, plus full-time childcare for her daughter. Those costs are top of mind as Escolastico, who voted for President Donald Trump in 2024, weighs whether to vote Democratic next month. She lives in Pennsylvania's hotly contested 7th Congressional District, one of a handful that will determine which party controls Congress next year. The midterm elections have been dominated by anxiety over rising prices for gas, groceries and housing, a liability for Trump and his Republican Party. For millions of parents of young children, childcare is one of the largest strains on the family budget. Both parties are talking about childcare Childcare costs have rose faster than inflation from 2020 to 2024, with the U.S. average for full-time childcare topping $13,000 in 2025, according to Child Care Aware of America. About three-quarters of U.S. adults saw the expense of childcare as a “major problem” in the U.S., and 64% supported the federal government providing free- or low-cost childcare for children too young for public school, according to an AP-NORC poll from June 2025. In the 7th District north of Philadelphia, both candidates are making childcare part of their pitch to voters. Like Escolastico, about 16% of the district’s voters were undecided as of September, according to a poll from Franklin and Marshall College . Democratic nominee Bob Brooks, a retired firefighter, has campaigned on establishing universal prekindergarten, expanding full-day kindergarten, increasing funding for Head Start and making more working families eligible for federal childcare assistance. He’s cited his own experience pitching in on childcare for his two granddaughters. “The cost of caring for the people you love keeps climbing, and nobody in Washington seems to notice,” Brooks said in a news release. The incumbent, freshman Republican Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, himself a father of two kids under age 3, has embraced more modest approaches that rely on tax breaks to lower costs. He cosponsored a bill to expand the federal tax credit for childcare expenses. The proposal, ultimately folded into Trump's sweeping bill of tax breaks and cuts to social programs, also increased tax incentives for private employers who subsidize or provide childcare for their workers. "I will continue to work together with both sides to ensure that working families get the resources, representation, and support that they deserve," Mackenzie said in a statement. Trump himself had campaigned on cutting childcare costs by using tariff revenue, a plan that has yet to materialize. More recently, he expressed skepticism of federal money for childcare. “We’re fighting wars. We can’t take care of daycare,” Trump told an Easter luncheon. Childcare has become an increasingly urgent priority The urgency over early childhood policy was accelerated by the pandemic. Daycare closures and weekslong quarantines laid bare the necessity and financial precarity of the childcare industry. To keep providers open, the federal government spent more than $50 billion on the industry, funding staff training, higher wages, protective gear and childcare assistance for more families. In 2021, President Joe Biden, a Democrat, proposed offering subsidies to most American families so they would never pay more than 7% of their household income on childcare. It was narrowly defeated in Congress. Three years later, the last of the pandemic aid expired. Waitlists for childcare assistance exploded, forcing low-income households to sideline a parent from the workforce or forgo necessities to foot a childcare bill. Since then, more candidates have campaigned on childcare solutions. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democratic socialist, pledged to make childcare free for all residents. The Democratic governors of New Jersey and Virginia elected last year both campaigned on plans to increase childcare funding. The Democratic nominee for mayor in Washington, D.C., won the primary in June after proposing to cap childcare expenses at 7% of a household's income. With childcare prices rising, Lerin Hagenbuch of Allentown says she wonders why the country hasn't moved toward universal childcare. She recalled when she and her husband, a quality assurance manager, anxiously searched for childcare so she could return to her job as a special education teacher, only to find that some of their options would require her to take a second job. Her son is now in kindergarten, but childcare costs remain one of her top issues. She's a registered Republican, but hasn’t decided how to vote next month. “There are staff shortages everywhere," Hagenbuch said. “If these moms or dads who are staying at home were able to even work part time, what a shift that would be.” $60 million in election spending boosts childcare issues The Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy, which advocates for greater government support for paid leave, child care and elder care, hopes voters like Hagenbuch will side with Democrats, who have historically favored bigger-ticket childcare investments. The political action committee said it has spent $60 million this year backing Democrats in statehouse, congressional and governor's races, targeting voters in a dozen states with canvassing, ads and mailers. The campaign pursues voters from both parties who feel the cost of caring for a child or an aging parent is growing untenable. “This is something that every family is touched by,” said Phoebe Kilgour, the campaign’s deputy executive director. “And so when you talk to people about what candidates are gonna do to … lower the cost of care, it can be super persuasive.” A longtime preschool teacher, Becky Fisher of Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, earns less than $20 an hour. Much of her paycheck goes to pay for before- and after-school care for her two sons at the childcare center where she works. Fisher was raised in a conservative Christian household and registered as a Republican when she graduated from high school, voting for President George W. Bush's reelection. She switched parties and in 2024 voted for then-Vice President Kamala Harris, Democrats' unsuccessful nominee for president. This year, she's still deciding how to vote, but says she wants to back a congressional candidate who will do more than pay lip service to supporting families and teachers. Childcare and early education are among the lowest-paid professions in the nation. And many of the field’s workers are parents like her. “Every parent is exhausted,” Fisher said. ___ The Associated Press’ education coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. articles.title: A 'golden age' vs. 'we're working on it': Trump and Vance differ on the economy
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Bill Clinton famously said he could feel voters’ pain over the economy. But these days, when it comes to questions about high prices , President Donald Trump insists that the pain is his. “They hit me with affordability, and that’s the first time I ever heard the word used,” he complained in Nebraska earlier this month. The White House leaves Vice President JD Vance to use a softer touch. Last month in Texas, he admitted “there are people out there who are frustrated by the pace of progress." And during a CBS News town hall on Saturday, Vance said, “I recognize that gas prices are too high right now" and "we’re working on it.” Depending on which Republican is speaking, Americans are getting a different perspective on how bad things are with the economy. Trump says “the golden age of America is upon us.” Vance walks a tightrope to show that he knows voters are feeling an economic pinch while still selling them on Trump's agenda. The disconnect comes as Americans’ confidence in the economy sank to the lowest level in more than a decade this month, the average long-term U.S. mortgage rate jumped this month to its highest level in nearly three years and the unemployment rate ticked up last month . Recent economic data released this month shows that high gasoline prices are intensifying inflation and more expensive oil and gas have begun to push prices up in other parts of the economy. While most of Trump's supporters don't hold him at fault, some acknowledge that the president's penchant for salesmanship may not hit the mark. "I think he talks it up,” said Conda Little, a 76-year-old retiree who went to see Trump in Dalton, Georgia, on Friday. “I think Vance is more real.” Little takes the president at his word that he will achieve a victory over Iran in a way that benefits U.S. consumers back home. But she said it’s impossible to deny the fallout from the conflict. “Everybody’s real upset about the gas” and “groceries are out of sight,” she said. “It’s hard. It’s really hard,” she said, adding that, “I think that people need to hear the truth.” ‘We need to do more’ Trump is loath to acknowledge concerns. He told reporters earlier this month that he gives himself “an A+ on the government, on economics, on everything.” He has dismissed concerns about high costs, arguing that concerns about affordability are a “hoax.” “We’re in the golden age of America. So our nation is doing better now than ever before,” he told a crowd in Kentucky on Saturday while campaigning for Republican candidates. Trump has occasionally acknowledged that gas prices are high , but has called it “a small price to pay” for keeping the country and the world safe with the Iran war. Trump’s discordant message with one of the top concerns voters are voicing ahead of the midterm elections has seemed heightened by his fixation on beautifying Washington and building a large ballroom at the White House. During a visit this month to an economically struggling corner of Arizona, he regaled the crowd with the story about how he ended up with a luxury jet gifted by Qatar to use as Air Force One. Vance, as he crisscrosses the country, is quick to say that the administration has more work to do. To cast blame, the vice president often says that his administration’s Democratic predecessors put the country in such a deep hole that they need more time to climb out. To show empathy, he often references his own experience growing up in a working-class family in a Rust Belt town. That's far different from Trump, who comes from a wealthy family, is a billionaire and even joked during his speeches on Friday and Saturday that if people have lunch at his Mar-a-Lago club, "for $5,000, you’ll get one hamburger and a small dessert.” Vance, during a CBS News town hall that aired on Saturday, said: “I grew up in a working-class family. When gas prices were high, I know that it made my grandmother suffer, and I’m sure that you’re struggling with it in a variety of ways." When asked by the moderator about the mixed message he and Trump are giving on the economy, Vance said Trump was speaking about new investments coming into the country, but said the changes take time. “We need to do more, and we can certainly do better,” he acknowledged. Many Trump supporters trust his pitch Some voters said Trump’s rosy view on the economy turns them away, like Santiago Rodriguez, a 19-year-old Texas college student who will be voting for the first time this year. Rodriguez, who attended a campaign rally last week for Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, said he would consider voting for a Republican but not while Trump is in charge because he doesn’t grasp the high cost of living for Americans. “I think he’s out of touch, I think he’s never seen what a true day as a Texan or anybody in general who is in the working class,” Rodriguez said. Trump's most loyal supporters aren’t interested in blaming high prices on anything the president has done. Cindy Massengill, a 67-year-old who came to see Trump in Dalton, Georgia, said she felt he’s doing the best he can. “I’m positive that he’s got done more than any other president after the mess we were left with Obama and Biden,” she said. Mary Bunker, a 67-year-old Republican who attended Trump’s Monday rally near Wichita, Kansas, said she works multiple jobs, including as a waitress and DoorDash driver. She feels the pressure of high gas prices, but she likes the tax breaks that Trump signed into law last year and she doesn’t fault the way he speaks about economic concerns. “I think he’s a very good businessman,” Bunker said. “He’s been in business a long time, so I think he knows what he’s talking about.” ___ Associated Press writers Bill Barrow in Dalton, Georgia, Jesse Bedayn in San Marcos, Texas, and Nicholas Ingram in Park City, Kansas, contributed to this report. articles.title: Ramaswamy faces growing criticism over ad featuring Ohio rival's estranged mom
articles.summary: A chorus of condemnation from some Ohio politicians is growing against Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy over an attack ad produced by his campaign that featured his opponent's estranged mother criticizing her and questioning the years of abuse she endured as a child. The ad, which has not been aired on television but spread on social media, shows Dr. Amy Acton's estranged mother, Donna Stearns Arthur, criticizing Acton, calling her a liar and casting doubt on Acton's upbringing. Acton has been estranged from Arthur since 1978 when her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, faced a rape charge for sexually assaulting Acton when she was 12 years old. Cledith died in southern Pennsylvania and was never convicted of the charge, and Acton's mother stayed married to him until his death. A clip of the ad, which blogger The Rooster shared on social media on Oct. 19 , shows Arthur accusing her daughter of lying about Acton's upbringing, which included homelessness, neglect and abuse, and urging Ohioans not to vote for Acton. "It's not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy has a serious problem," Arthur says in the ad. "She is a liar. She lies about her past." Acton's brother, Phillip Stearns, condemned the ad, and said Ramaswamy "stooped to a despicable low" in attempting to turn Acton's abuse into a "political talking point." “After [Cledith] was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died," Stearns said of Arthur. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants." The Acton campaign released an ad later Oct. 20 of Acton's brother berating Ramaswamy over the ad, and saying that "Amy took the brunt of [the abuse]." More: Amy Acton’s brother slams ad featuring estranged mother Acton told WOSU that her mother is the one lying. "It's awful to see her this way, and it's even more incredible to see that my opponent [Ramaswamy] has taken advantage of someone who's clearly not well, who is older, and this is totally in line with who he is," Acton told WOSU. Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy's campaign, doubled down on support for the ad and accused Acton of being a "serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor." Ramaswamy later Oct. 20 acknowledged to the USA TODAY Ohio Statehouse Bureau that his campaign produced the ad. "Her mother has spoken out for years and I don't know Amy Acton's mother and I've never met Amy Acton either," Ramaswamy said. "What I do know is that Amy Acton has been repeatedly and serially dishonest during this campaign and for much of her record in public service and I do believe that that record deserves to be scrutinized." Several prominent Democrats – including State Rep. Allison Russo, D-Upper Arlington, who is running for Ohio Secretary of State, and Maple Heights Mayor Annette Blackwell, who is running for state auditor against Secretary of State Frank LaRose – called on Ohio Republicans in an Oct. 20 media release to condemn the ad, calling it a "new and unacceptable low in Ohio politics." "Every single Republican candidate running for statewide office should immediately and publicly denounce this ad," Russo and other Democrats said in the media release "Silence in the face of such destructive rhetoric is an endorsement of it. It is time to raise the standard of public discourse in Ohio and focus on the practical solutions our citizens deserve." David Axelrod, a political consultant and CNN analyst, also took to X to condemn Ramaswamy and said that he had an "unquenchable ambition" to become Ohio's next governor. "I've been around politics longer than [Ramaswamy's] been alive, and I don't think I've seen anything uglier," Axelrod wrote. Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy's campaign, doubled down on support for the ad and accused Acton of being a "serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor." articles.title: Supreme Court rulings have been 'destructive to our democracy,' Justice Kagan says
articles.summary: By Jan Wolfe WASHINGTON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - US Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday said the court's conservative majority has undermined democracy and "created a race to the bottom" in how congressional districts are drawn. Kagan, one of the court's ‌three liberals, told students at Catholic University's law school that the conservatives have enabled increased political polarization by not reining ‌in partisan gerrymandering, which involves states redrawing the boundaries of electoral districts based on the partisan leanings of voters to boost a political party's candidates. In recent years, Kagan ​said, "both political parties have been engaged in a race to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders, effectively depriving masses of citizens of their rights to voting equality." Partisan gerrymandering is driving political candidates "toward the extremes, because the only thing anybody has to worry about anymore is being primaried," Kagan said. "It is making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so," Kagan said. "In this election, and ‌the next election, we are seeing large states ⁠with substantial numbers of people who vote for Republicans and who vote for Democrats, and the states are going to be tried to turn all red or all blue in a way that I think is ⁠very destructive to our democracy." The court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, in April gutted a pillar of the Voting Rights Act, a landmark 1965 civil rights law that aimed to prevent racial discrimination in voting. That ruling prompted a frenzied round of redistricting across the South to eliminate US House ​of ​Representatives districts where Black voters make up a majority or near-majority, as ​Republican-led states scrambled to take advantage of the decision. ‌President Donald Trump's Republican Party is seeking to retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections. At Trump's urging, Republican-governed Texas redrew its electoral map last year in an effort to flip Democratic-held US House seats, while Democratic-led California then reconfigured its map to target Republican-held House seats. Kagan, an appointee of former Democratic President Barack Obama, said the court's conservatives did not appreciate the real-world impact of their April voting rights decision, or their June decision that struck down a cap on the amount of money parties can spend on campaigns with ‌input from candidates. "I think part of the reason why the court got it ​wrong was a lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences ​of their decisions," Kagan said. “I do think in all these ​areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political ‌system works and has created a democracy that doesn’t ​work as well as it should,” ​she added. Kagan added that the June decision on campaign finance regulation has created opportunities for donors to corrupt candidates. "The one place where the court has allowed campaign finance regulation to operate is to prevent quid pro quo corruption, kind of money ​for favors, and the court never seems to ‌see the opportunities for doing exactly that," Kagan said. “I think you know the people of America look around this political ​system and think that all this money, chasing all these political candidates, is a nightmare, and they’re right,” she ​said. (Reporting by Jan Wolfe; Editing by Andrew Chung and Stephen Coates) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/us-high-court-rulings-destructive-013650423.html

articles.title: Elon Musk ordered Starlink slowdown in Ukraine, sources say
articles.summary: A decision by Elon Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, people familiar with the matter told CBS News. The satellite service, which is used for drone operations, hitting certain targets and protecting sites in Ukraine, was slowed significantly last week. Musk held multiple conversations with administration officials leading up to the order, the sources said. He wanted clarity on the president's thinking on the matter. Musk has expressed distaste with his company being seen as profiting from the continued war between Russia and Ukraine. It's not clear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed. Musk licenses SpaceX's Starshield technology to the U.S. government. He said last week the U.S. controls who can access the technology and what level of service those users receive. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk, the world's richest person, wrote on X . Musk did not reply to a request for comment. CBS News has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment. The Wall Street Journal was first to report on Musk's order. The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some officials inside the administration, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications. Mr. Trump said Monday he was seeking details on who ordered the slowdown. "I don't know who it was, but I'd like to find out," he said. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday the Pentagon has not manipulated the service. "We haven't pulled anything back. There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to. And that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions, but nothing's changed from our view. We haven't made any directives or anything like that," Hegseth told reporters, adding that "we wish the Ukrainians, obviously, success." Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday there were still limits on Ukraine's Starshield service. What is Starshield? Starshield is a military-grade satellite network made by SpaceX for the U.S. government and its partners. It runs on similar technology to its civilian sister, Starlink. The U.S. government pays to use Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances. There is no working alternative to Starlink, which has put a massive constellation of low-earth satellites into orbit, and no direct competitor comes close. What happened in Ukraine? Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including a throttling effect that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions. Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr speed cap, that is, the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates faster than the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable. Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr. Strike drones equipped with Starshield cruise at 160 km/h or higher, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes. Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr, making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Zelensky said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Shahed attack drones. The Ukrainian leader wrote on X last week that "the Russians are trying to take advantage of the problems with Starlink in Ukraine, as our interceptor drones depend on this connection among other things." Zelensky has suggested there are still some restrictions. He told NBC News over the weekend the maximum speed was 161 km/hr, and he said Tuesday that he'd spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio about "the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored." The apparent restrictions drew swift pushback from U.S. lawmakers, with a bipartisan group of senators asking the Defense Department's internal watchdog to investigate last week. "There needs to be an investigation, we need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things," Republican Rep. Mike Turner of Ohio said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" over the weekend . Why have Trump and Zelensky clashed? Beyond the Starshield disruptions, Zelensky has said in recent days that Russia struck Ukraine without warning from the U.S. , and deliveries of key interceptor missiles to Ukraine have slowed down. A senior Pentagon official told CBS News on Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine." Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to seek an end to the Russia-Ukraine war. The U.S. president argues the war is responsible for high energy prices. His administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week. Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire. In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," and argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," as he urged both sides to make a deal while adding that the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin. "I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/elon-musk-ukraine-spacex-starshield-trump-administration/

articles.title: Major loss of California beaches predicted in latest climate forecast
articles.summary: Waves continue to hit homes on Oct. 13 in Long Beach. Storm waves have affected the Long Beach peninsula in recent weeks, causing damage to coastal homes. (Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times) As ocean levels rise, waves crash farther inland and the coast continues to crumble, Southern California is on track to lose 30 to 70% of its beaches over the next several decades. Almost half of all beach cliffs are likely to retreat by 30 to 80 feet by 2100. And a 1.6-foot increase in sea level rise by 2060 will leave low-lying coastal areas including the ports and Santa Monica, Venice and Redondo beaches particularly vulnerable to floods and storms, with one estimate predicting 15,000 people exposed in Los Angeles County. Those are just some of the dire findings in California’s Fifth Climate Change Assessment , a state-commissioned report that comes out every several years and details how climate change is expected to affect everything from public health to animal habitat to central touchstones of the California way of life. “There are things in there that are hard to digest, and hard to wrap our heads around,” said Abby Edwards, senior deputy director for the Governor’s Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation, which led the assessment. “I just hope that this can be a call to action to make sure we are still really doubling down on all of our climate mitigation goals.” The report updates the picture for California’s hotter future with a projected 4-degree Fahrenheit increase in average temperatures and 50% longer heat waves by the middle of the century. Even more warming is expected farther inland where temperatures are already highest. In the Los Angeles region , which makes up 43% of the state’s population and comprises Los Angeles and Orange counties and parts of the Inland Empire and Ventura, inland areas are expected to see the hottest day of the year exceed 115 degrees by mid-century. San Bernardino, which already saw August temperatures peak at about 109 degrees this year, is expected to see 120 days a year above 95 degrees, compared with 81 days historically. Climate change is not expected to change average precipitation overall, but it will become even more skewed and sporadic, so wet and dry years both will become more frequent in California, and droughts will last longer. The increased heat means the state will lose about 40%  of its snowpack by mid-century, an important water source from the Sierra Nevada on which Southern California relies. The city of L.A., which brings in water from elsewhere for the vast majority of its supply, will be getting 7 to 13% less in imports by mid-century because its other sources, too, are drying up. The total area that burns in fires each year will increase dramatically — 50% by mid-century — without changes in land management. The effect will be strongest in the mountains. Native chaparral, the shrubby natural landscapes of the foothills, are becoming stressed and being replaced by grasses and other fire-prone invasive plants. Changes in rain and snowfall could lead to more seasons like the ones before the 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires , during which unusually wet winters fueled lots of green plant growth that then became tinder dry over eight months without rain . And just as the Eaton fire set low-income Black families further back than those with more resources to rebuild, many of the changes in the state’s climate will hit the most vulnerable hardest. A legacy of discriminatory housing policies means many low-income communities of color live in the hottest areas farther inland. One in five people in the Los Angeles region are currently unable to afford to adequately cool their homes, and the report notes this will probably get worse as extreme heat ramps up and puts more strain on the electric grid. For years experts have laid out different pathways for how the world could seriously address climate change. The report authors also looked at how climate change could play out differently if the world burns more or fewer fossil fuels and puts in place stronger or weaker policies. For most of their projections, they focused on the scenario considered most likely without major interventions. Edwards struck an optimistic note about the potential for a different outcome. “The future is not predetermined,” she said. “This is about projecting out into the future about what could happen, and I think it helps us be really clear-eyed about the decisions that we need to make.” When it comes to adapting to climate change, she noted examples of things California is already doing, including “huge investments in the state in extreme heat, and thinking about how do we put shade over bus stops and green schoolyards.” Many communities along the coast have developed sea level rise plans that include building seawalls and planting trees and shrubs to stabilize the coast, she added. And there is work being done around how to better capture rain and stormwater to accommodate changing precipitation. “I think there are a lot of actions that we can take right now to prepare us,” she said. articles.title: Trump unveils fraud whistleblower rewards, but he gets to decide who gets paid
articles.summary: Washington — President Trump on Tuesday announced the federal government will compensate whistleblowers who report people defrauding the U.S. government and taxpayers, but said he will decide who gets paid. "I will be the arbitrator of all of these decisions," the president said during his Oval Office announcement with Vice President JD Vance, who heads up the administration's fraud task force, beside him. "In other words, I'll determine whether or not the person is deserving and I'll determine — and I will be very generous, believe me." Through the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, Mr. Trump said whistleblowers, who can be ordinary citizens, will be eligible to receive 1% of the amount of fraud they report, even if the reported fraud is $100 billion. America.gov/fraud , however, says successful whistleblowers will be paid up to $30,000, dependent upon the report resulting in criminal charges. Asked by CBS News for clarification, Mr. Trump said there is no limit to whistleblower compensation, and criminal charges aren't necessary. "That's the answer. I quit while I'm ahead," Vance joked. The president promised to be "fair" in his decisions. "You'll get your money immediately, but I'll make the determination," he continued. "So if two people are fighting over it, maybe they'll split it or maybe whatever, but I'll make that determination." The America.gov/fraud website says reports are encrypted and will go directly to the Treasury Department. It's not immediately clear who reviews reports, although the Department of Justice will administer the program. The first person to benefit from the program is Nick Shirley , a 20-something YouTuber who published a video alleging fraud at childcare centers in Minnesota. He stood alongside Mr. Trump in the Oval Office Tuesday and was presented with a $10,000 check. Some whistleblowers can already receive compensation from the False Claims Act, which allows some whistleblowers to be entitled to up to 25% to 30% of proceeds recovered. But the requirements are stringent. Vance said "99%" of the fraud they're finding isn't covered by the False Claims Act. Naomi Seligman, president of nonprofit Whistleblower Aid, was skeptical of Mr. Trump's announcement, saying the president "is more interested in hunting down whistleblowers." "If the president is truly interested in rooting out wrongdoing, Whistleblower Aid invites him to start by examining the violations perpetrated by his own administration, including senior officials," she said in a statement. "We would happily work with him on this vital accountability effort to help save our democracy." articles.summary: 电竞游戏市场的持续增长，正在吸引越来越多手机厂商加码。 10月21日，荣耀在杭州发布新一代电竞手机WIN2和WIN RT2。 其中，WIN2搭载第六代骁龙8超级至尊版芯片，CPU主频最高达5.01GHz，配合LPDDR5X Ultra内存和UFS 4.1闪存，进一步强化游戏性能。 散热是此次升级的重点。荣耀WIN2采用双风扇主动散热设计，配备立体风网散热架构。屏幕方面，WIN2系列搭载2K 185Hz高刷新率屏幕，支持40余款原生高刷游戏，并通过自研显示芯片和触控芯片改善游戏体验。 续航方面，WIN2搭载10100mAh电池，支持100W有线快充和80W无线快充；WIN RT2则将电池容量进一步提升至12070mAh。 这距离荣耀推出首代WIN系列，还不到一年。 其他厂商也在加快新品布局。9月底以来，iQOO16、一加16等电竞手机相继发布，分别围绕旗舰芯片、高刷新率屏幕和散热能力展开竞争。 去年已经十分热闹的电竞手机市场，今年仍在继续硬件竞赛。 只是，这场围绕性能展开的竞争恰好撞上了存储成本暴涨周期。 随着新一代产品上市，电竞手机的售价已经出现明显上探。以荣耀为例，2025年12月发布的首代WIN系列，12GB+256GB版本首销价为3999元，12GB+512GB、16GB+512GB版本分别为4399元和4699元。 此次发布的WIN2，相同配置的首销价分别上涨至5499元、6299元和6999元，较上一代分别增加1500元、1900元和2300元。 尽管荣耀通过国补等优惠将WIN2的到手价压低至4999元起，但从首销价来看，新一代产品的价格门槛已经明显抬高。定位相对亲民的WIN RT2，国补后则以3149元起售。 类似的变化也发生在一加和iQOO身上。 一加16 12GB+512GB、16GB+512GB和16GB+1TB版本首销优惠价分别为6499元、7199元和8199元，较一加15上述三个版本的首发价分别上涨1900元、2300元和2800元。 iQOO同样如此。去年10月发布的 iQOO15，12GB+256GB 版本首销价为 4199 元，今年 iQOO16 上涨至 5999 元；16GB+512GB 版本则从4999元上涨至7499元，涨幅分别为1800 元、2500元。 短短一年，多款游戏性能旗舰相同存储配置版本的首销价上涨了千元以上。 背后是持续攀升的存储成本。Counterpoint Research数据显示，2026年第二季度智能手机存储器价格环比上涨超过80%。与此同时，新一代旗舰芯片及其他硬件升级，也在推高整机成本。 对于长期围绕旗舰芯片、大内存和高性能配置展开竞争的电竞手机而言，成本压力尤为明显。 更大的挑战在于，智能手机市场早已进入存量竞争，消费者换机周期不断拉长。即便游戏机的性能持续升级，短期内要推动用户大规模提前换机，仍然存在难度。 这也使得手机之外的电竞设备，开始成为厂商拓展业务的重要方向。 此次荣耀一口气推出电竞平板、耳机，并将游戏手柄等产品纳入电竞产品矩阵，试图将电竞业务从单一手机延伸至更多设备。例如，电竞手柄可以与手机搭配使用，进一步提升玩家的操控体验。 当存储涨价推高手机价格、换机需求又难以在短期内快速释放，电竞手机厂商需要寻找新的增长路径。 这场持续多年的硬件竞赛，也开始从手机本身延伸至更广泛的电竞生态。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 全系押注自研电池，理想亮出三电底牌
articles.summary: 作者 | 周智宇 理想正在扩大自研电池的应用范围。 10月20日，在Power Day电动技术发布会上，理想宣布，推出覆盖电池、电驱、超充设备及自建充电网络的技术体系，名为“连山”，并承诺：因自研电池本身质量问题引发自燃、车辆达到报废标准的，将赔付同配置新车。 这项研发已持续多年。2020年，理想正式立项自研5C超充电池，同步启动电芯自研。今年6月，自研电池随全新L8量产交付，随后扩展至L6、i8等车型。公司计划在产能爬坡后，陆续覆盖全系。 随着车企深入电芯研发，它们与电池供应商如何分工，也引发了讨论。今年9月，宁德时代首席制造官倪军在品质全球开放月活动上表示：“会造车，不一定会造电池。还是要专业的人，做专业的事。”他强调的是制造一致性：一辆车有数百乃至上千颗电芯，电芯之间的差异会影响整包表现。 10月19日，李想也谈到了这个问题。他主张，专业供应商应深入理解产品，整车厂也应深入核心技术，产业需要“两条腿”走路。这番表态没有点名宁德时代，但交代了理想继续投入电池研发的立场。 理想实际采用的是电芯自研、伙伴生产的分工：自己负责电芯设计研发，由欣旺达、中创新航等伙伴生产，电池包则自研自制。9月28日，李想就曾反对“去宁德化”的说法，称宁德时代为“战友”。 专业电池厂继续承担制造，理想则希望更早参与设计，在电芯开发时就把整车的续航、充电和空间要求考虑进去，并打通电池制造与车辆使用的数据。 “我们可以买到全世界最好的零件，但我们买不到零件之间的‘默契’。”理想汽车总裁兼总工程师马东辉在10月20日晚间说。 为了兼顾快充和续航，理想调整了电芯材料，提高电池包集成度，并优化整车布局。按理想公布的数据，搭载自研5C三元锂电池的全新L8，CLTC纯电续航达到430公里；即将上市的2026款i6两驱版，CLTC续航达到780公里，较2025款提升8%。 理想在2021年开始规划新一代电驱平台，目前五合一电驱和碳化硅高压三合一电驱已量产。其中一项改动，是取消功率模块上的高压端子，缩短电流到达芯片的路径，以减少损耗和空间占用。理想称，这一结构可带来约30公里续航提升，为整车垂向布局释放24毫米空间。 理想用了四年开发相关技术和精密焊接工艺，试制超过一万套样品。公司在苏州、常州自建功率模块及电驱总成工厂，设备和产线投入7亿元，不含厂房建设费用。据理想披露，自研功率芯片量产一年以来，累计上车400万颗。 截至10月20日，理想已建成4200座超充站、超过2.3万根超充桩。理想计划在2027年春节前，将其中的5C超充枪数量翻倍至8300根。 此次公布的两项终身保障中，另一项针对碰撞或底盘剐蹭造成的自研电池起火。车辆达到报废标准的，理想将补足车损险保单保额与保险实际赔付之间的差额。 据理想介绍，电芯产线配备了在线CT，扫描电芯内部结构，再结合AI分析识别缺陷。从原材料、电芯制备到电池包装配，各环节采用统一标准进行质量检查。 有制造积累、却难以独自承担全部研发投入的电池企业，也有机会从车企自研中受益。车企提供电芯方案，供应商把产品做出来，再跟随新车型增加供货。这类合作如果多起来，一些电池厂商或许可以借助客户的研发能力，缩小与头部企业的差距。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 从7天到隔夜：中国政策利率换锚，影响几何？
articles.summary: 10月19日，人民银行行长潘功胜在金融街论坛上表示，将研究择机把公开市场主要操作品种期限由7天切换为隔夜，公开市场隔夜回购利率（DR001）将相应成为主要政策利率。此举意味着中国货币政策框架由数量型调控向以短端市场利率为核心的价格型调控转型再进一步。 此前，DR001已成为人民银行短期利率调控的目标利率，但公开市场主要操作品种和政策利率期限仍为7天，操作端与目标端存在明显期限错配。此次改革的核心，是推动政策利率、操作工具与市场基准利率在隔夜期限上对齐，减少期限错配对政策信号传导的干扰。 若DR001作为主要政策利率（当前约为1.25%），相较当前1.40%的7天期逆回购利率，利率锚将降低15个基点。尽管从市场定价角度看，这具备“类降息”效果，为市场利率下行提供空间，但也不宜简单等同传统降息。 因为隔夜利率天然低于期限更长的7天期利率，两者之间存在正常的期限溢价。因此，换锚究竟带来多大程度的实际宽松，仍取决于换锚后政策利率是否低于当前DR001，以及是否推动利率走廊中枢下移、改善流动性条件并压低短期利率预期，不能仅凭两个期限的利率差认定央行已实施15个基点的降息。 与换锚同步，人民银行还提出推动贷款利率定价基准多元化，允许财务能力较强的企业自主选择DR001或贷款市场报价利率（LPR）作为浮动利率贷款定价基准；逐步退出存贷款基准利率；设立应对非银机构大额赎回的流动性支持工具；扩大常备借贷便利（SLF）适用机构范围至境内外资法人银行等。 政策利率与市场目标期限错配，利率市场化改革进入深化阶段

articles.title: 机构海外调研遭遇监管警示：展会缺席，娱乐在场？
articles.summary: 2026年3月，一家中型券商组织部分买方机构人员赴美，名义上是参加行业展会，但彼时拉斯维加斯并无相关展会安排，一行人实际是前往博彩场所娱乐。 当时，这起事件在市场内仅仅掀起过一阵讨论的浪花，但行业内的余波远未停息。 监管部门于2026年10月下发《机构监管情况通报》，针对境外调研违规、券商替基金支付海外差旅与专家费等乱象，公开对3家券商、2家基金公司依法采取监管措施，严查“券商垫付、佣金还账”的交易费用灰色链条。 由此，一些原本远离大众视线的情况，逐渐暴露出来。 监管点名部分机构违规 《通报》点名了近期部分机构的违规现象：一是部分基金公司境外调研的门票及专家咨询费由券商承担，反映出机构内控失效；二是个别基金从业人员私自出国游玩的机票和酒店费用由券商支付，已构成违反廉洁从业规定的行为。 根据检查情况，监管对存在不配合检查情形的G1证券公司采取监管谈话的监管措施，对公司副总裁兼研究所总经理胡某、以及研究所副所长孔某采取监管谈话的监管措施（后有媒体报道称或为国联民生证券的胡又文、孔蓉），并责令公司从严处分； 对H、G2证券公司和F、H基金公司采取出具警示函的监管措施；对H基金公司基金经理马某采取责令改正的监管措施，并要求公司严肃内部追责。 针对上述问题，监管层明确要求：各证券基金机构必须全面排查整改，把违规报销或超标的钱款退回，并对违规人员予以内部追责。 行程和调研费用是关键 海外调研是近年我国产业链出海、科技成长股投资日趋国际化后投研团队的必然需要，但随着类似调研的频次增多，也有一些不太合规的情况发生。 此前就有媒体报道提及，有券商在海外某国并无相关行业展会安排的情况下，仍组织买方机构出国调研，名义是走访海外产业链，但实际行程中却包括了安排观看世界杯赛事。 另外，还有行业内显示，另有券商组织赴日本考察MLCC（片式多层陶瓷电容器）产业链，但在调研过程中，部分买方基金经理和研究员在兑换日元后便自行离队。 这些案例的共同点在于，行程中掺杂了与投研无关的娱乐活动。在活动性质上或招待等级上，安排超出正常投研的服务范畴。 调研费用该如何分配和承担？ 那么合规路径下，海外调研中产生的部分费用，该如何分摊呢？ 业内通常认为，属于基金公司开展投研业务的运营成本，工具软件等费用，通常应由基金公司用其自有资金支付，不能转嫁给券商或基金资产。 此前，关于基金资产提取分仓佣金的比例和覆盖范围曾经有许多讨论和非议。在有关监管的牵头推动下，不仅分仓佣金费率有明显的降低，佣金使用范围也有收窄。比如，常用的数据和研究系统、专家交流费用等最新就不被列入了。 而此次涉及的，券商先以行业展会等名义立项，再邀请基金经理、研究员参加，使行程获得业务合理性；随后由券商垫付境外调研的门票及专家咨询费等开支的做法，确实并不合乎最新的规定。 如何确定卖方服务边界 此次事件，还催生了投资业内对于调研流程和工作范围的讨论。 怎样的调研费用是合理费用，什么环节是调研费用可以覆盖的，怎样是不能覆盖的，这些边界其实过去一直不那么清晰，行业也正在呼唤更清晰的边界。 前期提到的赌场、世界杯现场当然并不合适，但如果涉及到消费个股的调研，那么具体店铺、网点的调研可能是需要的。 过高的招待标准显然是不合适，并有利益输送嫌疑的。但正常的调研又是需要的，究竟费用该如何区分合理程度呢？ 海外资管行业有一些较为成熟的经验，其一，公司内部设立"原则+内部制度+登记+审批"的制度体系，通过组织流程和多环节把控来保证费用支出的合理性。 其二、对于交通行程安排上，原则上有成熟航班安排的地区间交通，基金经理应自负费用，如遇到矿区/厂区之类必须由组织方安排包机的，则由组织方承担，但基金经理应报备留痕。 其三、对于出于调研效率需要的本地交通（比如包大巴）、提供工作简餐等，属于合理范畴。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: SpaceX与特斯拉合并，马斯克在下一盘多大的棋？
articles.summary: SpaceX交出一份很难再用"火箭公司"概括的成绩单：第三季度，SpaceX营收146亿美元，同比增长161%，净利润44亿美元，超出分析师平均预期逾一倍。 财报电话会上，马斯克确认：SpaceX和特斯拉已分别成立由独立董事组成的特别委员会，讨论可能的合并。两家公司合并估值约3.5万亿美元。 马斯克先说自己是在"雷区里跳踢踏舞"。几秒之后还是给了答案，合并"有很多好处"。 Deepwater Asset Management 的 Gene Munster 事后数了数，这句话他讲了大概三遍。 这让一个谈论已久的设想进入了正式评估阶段：彭博指出，特斯拉市值约 1.5 万亿美元，SpaceX 约 2 万亿美元，合在一起 3.5 万亿。 会不会合并，已经不该是问题。巴克莱在 10 月 14 日的报告认为， 两家合并的可能性"已经越来越成为共识预期"。 股东名册高度重叠，SpaceX 买特斯拉的 Cybertruck，又通过 xAI 买公用事业级储能电池。今年 9 月的 All-In 峰会上，马斯克被问到为什么两家公司要分开，他反问："这么多层面都在合作，谁能想象在如此紧密的合作下会采取什么行动。" 消息传出后，SpaceX盘后涨幅约8%，特斯拉仅涨约1.8%——收购方涨得比被收购方更多。这一差异反映出两类股东截然不同的盘算，也预示着这笔交易在正式落地之前，还有漫长的博弈要走。 SpaceX的AI业务已大到无法当作副业 SpaceX第三季度的收入结构说明了合并讨论为何在此时升温。 人工智能及算力业务收入75.6亿美元，较上年同期增长逾九倍，已首次超过Starlink所在的连接业务， 季度营业利润从去年同期亏损17亿美元转为盈利4.31亿美元。连接业务营收52.5亿美元，同比增长69%，目前仍贡献更多利润，但增速明显慢于AI业务。相比之下，设计、制造和运营火箭与飞船的传统发射业务营收17.7亿美元，仅增长6%。 增长的另一面是开支。 第三季度，SpaceX资本支出接近196亿美元，其中AI及算力业务约164亿美元。 前九个月，公司经营现金流约131亿美元，购置物业、厂房及设备支出约481亿美元。单看44亿美元的季度净利润，很容易低估算力设施建设所需的真实资金规模。据报道，SpaceX正在洽谈借款400亿美元用于采购英伟达芯片，CFO Bret Johnsen表示公司会继续举债，"有好几个可用的债务资金池正在谈"，并给出明年一季度总营收最高370亿美元的指引。 SpaceX目前已是Anthropic、Alphabet等公司的主要算力与基础设施供应商，8月还收购了代码编辑工具Cursor。一家收入结构里AI占比最高、正在大举举债买卡的公司，用"火箭公司"来定义已经远远不够。 协同逻辑清晰，但股权合并未必是唯一路径 马斯克列举的合作清单涵盖超级智能软件、芯片设计、Terafab、机器人、轨道数据中心和连接服务。这些项目不断碰到同一批资源： 芯片、能源、制造能力，以及能够持续支付建设成本的资本。 "简化决策"是合并动机中排名靠前的一项——许多跨公司项目需要两个董事会和两批股东分别点头。 Terafab是其中最具体的节点。按巴克莱测算，特斯拉计划先在奥斯汀建一座约30亿美元的研究设施，随后跟进约168亿美元的生产厂，两家公司很可能共同出资。这里产出的芯片将供给特斯拉自动驾驶汽车和擎天柱机器人，同时也供给SpaceX的AI与轨道数据中心。马斯克此前已明确表示，Terafab的决策需要两家董事会各自审批，"可能要花一阵子"，目标是2028年底量产。 10月15日亮相的新款Roadster搭载了SpaceX开发的冷气推进器，可完成倒退上坡、空中转向等动作。 Gene Munster对那场发布会的评价是"一次工程炫技"，并说马斯克"等不及"要合并。 然而，业务能够深度合作，并不能直接证明股权必须合并。特别委员会需要回答的核心问题是：合作产生的新增价值是否足以抵消交易成本、监管摩擦和整合风险。 "特斯拉为SpaceX输血"的叙事，数字并不支撑 合并传闻中，一个直观的说法是： SpaceX大建AI基础设施，特斯拉可以提供现金流。这一说法抓住了SpaceX资本开支庞大的事实，却高估了特斯拉眼下可供调配的资金。 据彭博一致预期，特斯拉2030年自由现金流约120亿美元，而SpaceX预计届时消耗约170亿美元——两者方向相反。更近的数字同样不乐观：特斯拉第二季度自由现金流为负11亿美元；分析师预测其第三季度自由现金流均值为负45亿美元，2026年全年约为负97亿美元。与此同时，SpaceX截至9月底持有约513亿美元现金及386亿美元有价证券，资金状况并不匮乏。 合并不会凭空增加一美元现金，它可能改变的是融资方式和资本配置权限——哪些项目由合并后的公司统一建设，哪些成本由不同业务共同承担，以及投资者愿意为这一整套计划提供多少资本。 对马斯克而言，统一配置资源或许更高效；对特斯拉股东而言，问题在于汽车、储能和机器人业务创造的价值，将如何分配给SpaceX的算力、卫星和航天项目。若交易方案说不清这一点，"协同"反而会成为资本开支失控的担忧。 控制权结构，可能是交易设计里最关键的一笔 分析师普遍认为，这笔交易在经济利益之外还有另一层逻辑—— 控制权 。 巴克莱测算，马斯克持有SpaceX约48%的经济权益，通过每股10倍投票权的B类股掌握约82%的投票权；在特斯拉持股约20%，折算后接近17%的投票权。若SpaceX按当前估值以换股方式收购特斯拉，他在合并后公司中大约持有37%的经济权益，控制约56%的投票权。RBC的口径稍有差异，认为马斯克掌握SpaceX 85%的投票权，但方向一致：交易会把"经济权益不到四成、投票权过半"这个结构复制到一家3.5万亿美元量级的公司身上。 马斯克曾公开表示，他希望持有特斯拉约25%的股权，才足以维持对AI和机器人战略的影响力，而目前仍有差距。这笔交易可以利用SpaceX的双层股权结构补上这个缺口。 这一点直接影响谈判难度。马斯克本人已承认存在利益冲突，不能参与特别委员会的讨论。委员会不仅要评估业务协同，还要确定各自估值、换股比例、可能的溢价，以及不同类别股东在合并后各自拥有多少经济权益和投票权。 真正握着否决权的，是华盛顿 路透社将地缘政治和监管列为合并的"最大挑战"： SpaceX是美国军方、情报机构和NASA的主要承包商，Starshield已被用于战场通信，马斯克和特朗普均否认对其设限，但这套系统的军事敏感性已毋庸置疑。 因此，对合并的审查维度将从反垄断扩展到国家安全。反垄断审查、双方股东与董事会批准、外国投资审查，三道程序中任何一道卡住，交易的形态都会发生变化。这种类型的交易在商业史上没有先例，也不存在现成的监管模板。 盘面给出答案，但定价有待细化 特别委员会消息确认后，SpaceX盘后最多涨约8.6%，特斯拉仅涨约1.8%，SPCX盘前一度报161.18美元，较收盘价高约9%。 Space Capital的Chad Anderson给出了一种叙事： 合并后的公司将是唯一拥有完整"物理AI栈"的企业，从芯片制造到轨道数据中心，再到地面自主设备，没有竞争对手有对应的完整体系。 他的机构是SpaceX的早期投资人。 RBC给予特斯拉480美元的目标价，较368美元附近的收盘价隐含不到三成的上行空间。对于特斯拉股东而言，算盘并不难打：用确定性的汽车周期换成一家AI算力公司的长期期权。但这笔换算是否划算，取决于换股比例和合并后的资本分配方案，而这两份文件目前都还不存在。 值得注意的是，作为收购货币的SPCX于今年6月IPO，定价135美元，首日开盘150美元，四个月后股价基本回到起点。用一只上市不久的股票作为收购对价，其定价基准仍主要依赖投行模型，二级市场尚未经过反复交易的充分检验。若只有愿景继续升温而交易条款迟迟缺席，股价反应很难替代对换股比例和资本计划的实质审查。 眼下最该盯的四件事 首先，是特别委员会的构成与独立性。 两家公司都表示由独立董事组成委员会，但成员是谁、有无聘请独立财务顾问、顾问是否出具公允意见，将决定这份方案在股东眼里是"马斯克的意思"还是"董事会的判断"。 其次，12月3日股东年会如何使用。 特斯拉已将2026年股东年会定于12月3日。按目前披露的信息，不能将这场年会视为已安排好的合并投票。赶在年会前宣布交易意向，反对票更容易组织；错开宣布，则面临更长的监管窗口和更多变数。巴克莱的分析称，若选在10月底或11月初宣布，股东在年度会上投赞成票反而更难——这与"抢在窗口关闭前生米煮成熟饭"的直觉正好相反。 接着，那400亿美元借款的条款与时序。 若这笔资金在合并敲定之前先行落地，意味着SpaceX打算在交易完成前就锁定算力资本开支，合并对SpaceX的意义就更偏向补充现金流，而非共同投资。 最后，Terafab和特斯拉财报的实际数字。 得州设施的土地、环评、设备订购，任何一环慢下来，2028年底量产目标就要后移。而特斯拉第三季度财报将同期呈现资本支出、自由现金流，以及管理层对Terafab、机器人和算力投资的最新表态——若现金消耗继续扩大，股东对合并后资本纪律的要求只会更高。 马斯克想推进的，可能是一家从芯片和能源供给，到算力、连接网络，再到机器人应用都能自行协调的公司。 这盘棋有多大，已经能从SpaceX的收入结构和投资规模中看见。它能否让股东受益，则要等特别委员会拿出价格、治理安排和可核算的协同收益。眼下最该盯的，是特斯拉财报里的现金流，以及两家公司下一份正式交易文件。 风险提示及免责条款
